claim: `REG[#myregs + index]` (register_access code block, the primary defect class reg-hash-in-register-index), its notes ('# returns cog register address', 'REG[] accesses cog memory') and the addressing_mode_comparison row `syntax: "REG[#myreg]"` (:180) give a form the compiler rejects. REG[] takes the register symbol itself and a separate [index]: `REG[myregs][index]` compiles; `REG[#myregs]` and `REG[myregs + index]` (run-time index inside the brackets) both fail with 'Expected a constant, unary operator, or "("'. `#myregs` as a free-standing term (`x := #myregs`) is legal and gives the cog address.
SCAS is described as 'Signed scale: (a * b) >> 32'. The source gives SCA as (x * y) >> 32 and SCAS as (x * y) >> 30.

REV is described 'Reverse bottom N bits, zero the rest' with `%1010_0011 REV 8  ' Returns %1100_0101`. `x REV y` reverses bits 0..y, i.e. y+1 bits, so REV 8 reverses nine bits ($18A); the shown result %1100_0101 is `REV 7`. The same file's changed_from_p1 row (:357) states the rule correctly ('REV (n-1) -- REV takes the top bit index'), so the page contradicts itself.

claim: next_power_of_two: `result := DECOD ENCOD (n - 1)  ' Round up to next power of 2`. ENCOD returns the index of the highest set bit, so DECOD ENCOD x is the highest power of two NOT ABOVE x: n=5 gives ENCOD 4 = 2, DECOD 2 = 4 (should be 8); n=4 gives 2 (should be 4). The round-up needs one more: `DECOD (ENCOD (n - 1) + 1)` (n=1 and n=0 also need a guard). The block compiles, so no gate can see it.

The two C-precedence anti-patterns give `==` as 'level 13' and `+` as 'level 9'. In the operator table `==` (and the other comparisons) is level 11 and `+` is level 8; level 13 is `&&`/AND and level 9 is `#>`/`<#`. The conclusions (& and << bind tighter than == and +) are right; the quoted levels are not.

The overview lists 'swap (:=:)' among the assignment operators and the swap_values pattern is `a :=: b  ' a and b are swapped`. `:=:` swaps two STRUCTURE variables (v45); on plain long variables it does not compile ('Variable needs an operator'); the swap of two longs is `a, b := b, a`. (Primary defect class swap-operator-on-plain-variables.)

'float operations are slow (~100x integer)' and '?? Random number (XORO32 hardware)'. No source gives a 100x ratio (floating_point.yaml:103-111 itself says the KB publishes no per-operation figure). `??var` is a Spin2 bytecode that executes the PASM XORO32 instruction on the interpreter's cog; the operator also requires a variable (see defect xoro-operator-without-variable).

'The ?? operator implements XORO32 (xoroshiro32+): state ^= state >> 2; state ^= state << 1; state ^= state >> 1; return state' with 'Period: 2^32 - 1 (never produces zero from non-zero seed)', 'Zero seed produces zero forever'. No source states this algorithm; the silicon doc only lists the XORO32 instruction, and the source says `??var` iterates a long 'per XORO32'. The pseudo-code is a plain xorshift, not a xoroshiro32 variant; the period and zero-state statements are unsourced. (The seed-must-be-nonzero advice may well be right for an xoroshiro-family generator, but it is an inference, not a documented fact.)

(a) modulo_bias: `GETRND() // 10  ' Slight bias toward 0-5`: `//` is the SIGNED remainder, so a negative GETRND value yields a negative remainder (-9..9); the defect is the sign, not a bias toward 0-5. (b) truncating_without_scaling: the 'correct' form `GETRND() +// 256  ' Full 32-bit randomness` is the low 8 bits of GETRND -- the same bits as the 'wrong' form `GETRND() & $FF  ' Only uses low 8 bits`; the comment contradicts the anti-pattern's own premise. (c) random_float: `FLOAT(GETRND()) /. 4294967295.0  ' [0.0, 1.0)`: FLOAT converts the long as a SIGNED integer, so half the results are negative [inferred: the source says only 'convert integer x to float']; and 2^32-1 is not representable in single precision (it rounds to 2^32).

claim: single_pin_operations says PINREAD returns 'TRUE (-1) if high, FALSE (0) if low'; pinread.yaml:13 says 'For single pin: returns 0 or 1', and the interpreter's PINREAD zero-extends the pin field to the field width (1 bit for a single pin): the value is 0 or 1. The button_read example `IF !PINREAD(BUTTON_PIN)` then tests a bitwise NOT of 0/1 = -1/-2, which is ALWAYS non-zero -- the 'press detected' branch runs every pass. Correct: `IF NOT PINREAD(BUTTON_PIN)` or `PINREAD(BUTTON_PIN) == 0`. The block compiles.

range_operator: `syntax: bottom_pin..top_pin`, `example: 8..15 = pins 8 through 15`, 'Wraps if top_pin < bottom_pin'. The Spin2 pin range is written TOP..BOTTOM: `PINLOW(49..40)` is pins 49..40, and `Top < Bottom` wraps. Compiled: `pinlow(15..8)` and `pinlow(8 addpins 7)` produce byte-identical binaries (md5 d74383f6...), `pinlow(8..15)` produces a different one (base 15 with 25 extra pins, wrapping within the block).

anti_pattern rdpin_blocking_forever: 'RDPIN blocks until data ready - may hang if no data arrives'. RDPIN does not wait: the instruction reads the smart pin's Z and acknowledges, and the Spin2 RDPIN is that single instruction. A read when no new data is present returns the last value. The 'correct' form (poll PINREAD or time out first) is a reasonable pattern, but the stated hazard is not the documented behaviour.
source: engineering/ingestion/sources/silicon-doc/silicon-doc-text.txt:3720 (`RDPIN D,S/# {WC} - Get smart pin S/# result Z into D, flag into C, ack pin`); engineering/ingestion/external-inputs/source-code/spin-interpreter/v51/Spin2_interpreter.spin2:1098 (`rdpin_ rdpin x,x wc`, no wait)

claim: critical_rule: 'Behavior undefined if COGs drive conflicting states (not documented in P2 spec)'; hardware_note: 'No documented conflict resolution, wire-OR, or priority scheme'. The Silicon Doc documents it: the DIR and OUT bits of all cogs are OR'd before going to the pins (and the smart-pin write buses likewise).
source: engineering/ingestion/sources/silicon-doc/silicon-doc-text.txt:3725 ('Each smart pin OR's all incoming 34-bit buses from the cogs in the same way DIR and OUT bits are OR'd before going to the pins')

claim: `debug(@"Hello, World!")`, `debug(STRING("Line 1", 13, 10, "Line 2"))`, `debug(label_ptr, ": ", UDEC(value))`, `debug(@msg_success)`: inside DEBUG() a bare numeric term is a CHARACTER ('comma-separated strings and characters ... DEBUG("...", 13, 13)'); a string at a pointer is printed with ZSTR(ptr). These calls compile with -d but print one character (the pointer's low byte), not the string. Correct: `debug(zstr(@"Hello"))`, `debug(zstr(label_ptr), ": ", udec(value))`. [inferred from the source's DEBUG rules; not bench-verified]

The 'PUB/PRI parameters' and 'return values' rules, the summary_table rows, common_mistakes (`PUB foo(BYTE a, b)  ' Expecting both to be BYTE`) and the note 'non-sticky behavior prevents accidental type truncation of parameters' all assume BYTE/WORD-typed parameters and results exist. They do not: parameters/results are longs or pointers (`^BYTE`, `^WORD`, `^LONG`, `^StructName`); `BYTE a` in a parameter or result list does not compile. Only the local-variable and VAR/DAT rows are true. (Primary defect class byte-word-typed-parameter-or-result.)

us_to_cycles: 'us-scale ceiling is ~2.1B us at 200 MHz -- rarely a practical concern'. `clkfreq / 1_000_000 * us` is 200 * us at 200 MHz; it overflows signed 32-bit at us > 2^31 / 200 = ~10.7 million us (~10.7 s) -- the same ceiling as the ms variant two lines above. 2.1B is the cycle count (2^31), not a microsecond count.

claim: archetype pasm_only_object: 'Contains only DAT section with PASM code, loaded and called by parent via COGINIT'; 'No Spin2 methods, only DAT/PASM'; parent_usage `COGINIT(COGEXEC_NEW, @pasm_calc.pasm_entry, @params)`. PNut-TS rejects a DAT-only file used as an OBJ ('fast_calculator.spin2 is a PASM file and cannot be used as a Spin2 object'), and with a PUB present it rejects `@pasm_calc.pasm_entry` ('Expected an object constant, structure, or method'): a parent reaches a child's methods and constants, not its DAT labels. The working form hands the address out through a child method (verified: `PUB entry_addr() : a / a := @pasm_entry`; `pasm_calc.entry_addr()`).

The JonnyMac naming standard asks for UPPERCASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES constants and lowercase variables and its examples use the same words for both: constant `RX_PIN`/`TX_PIN` beside variable `rx_pin`/`tx_pin` (constant_documentation vs variable_documentation; complete_constant_section vs complete_variable_section). Spin2 names are case-insensitive, so they are the same name: put together in one object, `long rx_pin` fails with 'Expected a unique variable name... (m240)' (reproduced by compiling variable_documentation.example after constant_documentation.example). Each block compiles alone, which is why the gate is green; the standard as a whole does not hold.

claim: The complex_method template writes `wypin(txbyte, TX_PIN)` (data first, pin second) -- the PASM2 operand order. The Spin2 method is WYPIN(PinField, Data): pin first (basic-io.yaml:456-463 states exactly this).
